claims.text: Premelting and melting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are governed by surface segregation of relatively low-melting-point elements.
Surface segregation creates a compositionally enriched, weakly bound shell.
The segregated shell melts below the melting temperature of the bulk alloy.
Colloidal synthesis or physical vapor deposition can yield uniformly and randomly mixed 5- or 7-element high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Thermal annealing under an inert atmosphere promotes atomic diffusion and surface segregation.
The proposed annealing treatment can alter surface composition without significantly affecting core stoichiometry.
A heating rate of approximately 5 °C/min is slow enough to capture subtle premelting transitions.
Surface enrichment in lower-melting-point elements produces an effective core-shell structure with a shell melting temperature below that of a uniformly mixed nanoparticle.
Thermally activated diffusion preferentially relocates lower-melting-point elements to the nanoparticle surface.
This segregation reduces surface cohesive energy.
Reduced surface cohesive energy initiates premelting at the nanoparticle surface.
Surface-initiated melting propagates inward as temperature increases.
Annealed, surface-segregated nanoparticles will have a lower premelting-onset temperature than quenched, uniformly mixed nanoparticles.
Annealed, surface-segregated nanoparticles will have a broader melting transition than the quenched baseline.
The magnitude of melting-temperature depression will correlate with the extent of surface enrichment in lower-melting-point elements.

The proposed mechanism is expected to hold for high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles between 5 and 20 nm that contain at least one element with a substantially lower melting point than the other constituents.
The mechanism may not apply when constituent melting points are closely matched.
The mechanism may not apply when particle-size effects dominate melting behavior.
